title: Modifying Data, Schema & Performance
description: Insert, update, and delete data; define tables with constraints; use transactions safely; speed up queries with indexes; and bring it all together in a capstone report

lessons.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
lessons.description: Add, change, and remove rows — the three ways SQL modifies data

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements, and explain why WHERE matters so much on the last two.

sections.title: ➕ INSERT: adding new rows
sections.content:
`INSERT` adds a new row to a table by listing the columns and their values:

```sql
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, signup_date)
VALUES ('Priya Shah', 'priya@example.com', 'Austin', '2026-01-15');
```

The column list and the values list must line up one-to-one, in the same order. Any column you leave out gets its default value (or NULL, if it allows one).

sections.title: ✏️ UPDATE: changing existing rows
sections.content:
`UPDATE` changes the values in rows that already exist:

```sql
UPDATE products
SET price = 24.99
WHERE product_id = 101;
```

**The WHERE clause here is critical.** Without it, `UPDATE` changes **every row in the table** — there's no built-in "are you sure?" step. Always double-check your WHERE clause (ideally by running it first as a SELECT) before running an UPDATE.

sections.title: 🗑️ DELETE: removing rows
sections.content:
`DELETE` removes whole rows from a table:

```sql
DELETE FROM orders
WHERE status = 'cancelled' AND order_date < '2025-01-01';
```

Just like UPDATE, `DELETE` without a `WHERE` clause removes **every row** in the table. This is one of the most common — and most damaging — mistakes in SQL, so it's worth building the habit of writing and checking the WHERE clause before you even think about the DELETE keyword.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Running UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause and affecting the entire table. Not testing the WHERE condition as a SELECT first, to see exactly which rows would be hit, before running the UPDATE or DELETE for real.

questions.question: What happens if you run UPDATE products SET price = 0; with no WHERE clause?
options: Nothing changes, since WHERE is required
Every row in the products table gets its price set to 0
Only the first row is updated
It only affects rows where price was already 0
questions.explanation: Without a WHERE clause, UPDATE applies to every single row in the table — this is one of the most common and costly SQL mistakes.

questions.question: What's a good habit before running a risky UPDATE or DELETE?
options: Run it directly, then check the results
Run the same WHERE condition as a SELECT first, to see exactly which rows would be affected
Always add ORDER BY
Avoid using WHERE entirely to keep the query simple
questions.explanation: Testing the WHERE condition with a SELECT first lets you confirm exactly which rows would be touched, before making an irreversible change with UPDATE or DELETE.

questions.question: In INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Sam', 'sam@example.com');, what determines which value goes into which column?
options: Values are matched alphabetically to column names
The order of the VALUES list matches the order of the column list, position by position
SQL guesses based on data type
It's random unless ORDER BY is used
questions.explanation: The column list and VALUES list are matched by position: the first value goes to the first listed column, the second value to the second column, and so on.

questions.question: What does INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... let you do that a plain INSERT with VALUES cannot?
options: Insert exactly one row at a time
Insert multiple rows copied or computed from the result of a query
Delete rows before inserting
Update existing rows
questions.explanation: INSERT INTO ... SELECT lets you populate a table with however many rows a query produces, rather than typing out literal VALUES for each row.

questions.question: If a column has a NOT NULL constraint and you try to INSERT without providing a value for it (and no default), what happens?
options: The value defaults to an empty string
The insert fails with a constraint violation
The value defaults to 0
SQL silently skips that column
questions.explanation: A NOT NULL column with no default and no supplied value causes the INSERT to fail, since the database can't leave it empty.

questions.question: What's the difference between DELETE FROM table and TRUNCATE TABLE?
options: They are identical in every database
DELETE removes rows one by one and can be filtered with WHERE; TRUNCATE removes all rows at once and typically can't be filtered
TRUNCATE only works on empty tables
DELETE cannot be used with WHERE
questions.explanation: DELETE supports WHERE to remove specific rows and is logged row-by-row, while TRUNCATE quickly clears the entire table and generally doesn't accept a WHERE clause.

questions.question: In UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE order_id = 42;, what rows are affected?
options: Every row in the orders table
Only the row where order_id equals 42
No rows, since UPDATE needs two conditions
Only rows shipped previously
questions.explanation: The WHERE clause restricts the UPDATE to just the row(s) matching order_id = 42, leaving every other row untouched.

questions.question: Why might you wrap an UPDATE affecting many rows in a transaction with BEGIN/COMMIT?
options: Transactions are required for every UPDATE
So you can review the effect and ROLLBACK if something looks wrong before committing
It makes the UPDATE run without a WHERE clause
It automatically creates a backup table
questions.explanation: Wrapping a risky UPDATE in a transaction lets you inspect the results and roll back if they're not what you expected, before making the change permanent.

lessons.title: Creating Tables & Constraints
lessons.description: Define a new table's columns, types, and the rules that keep its data valid

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write a CREATE TABLE statement with appropriate data types and constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK).

sections.title: 🏗️ CREATE TABLE
sections.content:
`CREATE TABLE` defines a brand-new table — its columns, and each column's data type:

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name         TEXT NOT NULL,
  email        TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  city         TEXT,
  signup_date  DATE
);
```

**Common data types** you'll see everywhere: `INTEGER` (whole numbers), `TEXT`/`VARCHAR` (strings), `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC` (exact decimals — good for money), `DATE`/`TIMESTAMP` (dates and times), and `BOOLEAN` (true/false).

sections.title: 🚧 Constraints: rules the database enforces for you
sections.content:
Constraints aren't just documentation — the database actively rejects any change that would break them:

• `PRIMARY KEY` — uniquely identifies each row (implies NOT NULL + unique)
• `NOT NULL` — this column can never be left empty
• `UNIQUE` — no two rows may share the same value in this column
• `FOREIGN KEY` — this column must match an existing value in another table's primary key
• `CHECK` — a custom condition every row must satisfy

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
  total_amount DECIMAL CHECK (total_amount >= 0),
  status       TEXT NOT NULL
);
```

That `REFERENCES customers(customer_id)` is the foreign key constraint — it stops you from ever inserting an order for a customer_id that doesn't actually exist.

sections.title: 🛡️ Why constraints matter
sections.content: Constraints turn "we hope the application code always gets this right" into "the database itself guarantees it." A CHECK constraint on `total_amount >= 0` means a negative order total is *impossible*, no matter what inserts it — a bug in one part of an application can't silently corrupt data that constraints protect.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Skipping NOT NULL on columns that should always have a value, only to find NULLs causing problems much later. Choosing FLOAT for money instead of DECIMAL/NUMERIC — floating point math can introduce tiny rounding errors that matter for currency.

questions.question: What does the PRIMARY KEY constraint guarantee about a column?
options: It can contain duplicate values
Every value in it is unique, and it can never be NULL
It must always be a text column
It automatically indexes every other column too
questions.explanation: PRIMARY KEY combines uniqueness and NOT NULL — every row must have a value in that column, and no two rows can share the same one.

questions.question: What does customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id) enforce?
options: Nothing — REFERENCES is just a comment
customer_id can't be NULL, and must match an existing customer_id in the customers table
customer_id must be unique across all orders
It automatically creates a new customer row if one doesn't exist
questions.explanation: This combines NOT NULL (a value is required) with a foreign key reference (REFERENCES), which requires the value to already exist as a customer_id in the customers table — protecting against orders pointing at nonexistent customers.

questions.question: Why is DECIMAL usually preferred over FLOAT for storing money?
options: DECIMAL is always faster to compute with
FLOAT can introduce small rounding errors that matter for exact currency values, while DECIMAL stores exact values
FLOAT can't store negative numbers
There's no real difference between them
questions.explanation: Floating-point types are optimized for a wide range of values but can introduce tiny rounding imprecision. DECIMAL/NUMERIC types store exact values, which is important when every cent needs to be exactly correct.

questions.question: What does the UNIQUE constraint enforce on a column, as opposed to PRIMARY KEY?
options: Exactly the same thing as PRIMARY KEY, with no differences
No duplicate values, but unlike PRIMARY KEY it can typically allow NULL
That the column must be numeric
That the column is indexed but not enforced
questions.explanation: UNIQUE prevents duplicate values like PRIMARY KEY does, but a table can have multiple UNIQUE columns and, in most databases, UNIQUE columns can contain NULL while PRIMARY KEY cannot.

questions.question: What does a DEFAULT value on a column do?
options: Forces every insert to explicitly provide that value
Automatically fills in that value when an INSERT doesn't specify one for that column
Prevents NULLs from ever appearing
Deletes rows missing that column
questions.explanation: A DEFAULT supplies an automatic value for the column whenever an INSERT statement doesn't explicitly set it.

questions.question: What does a CHECK constraint let you enforce?
options: That a column must reference another table
A custom condition a column's value must satisfy, such as price >= 0
That a column is always unique
That a table has at least one row
questions.explanation: CHECK constraints let you define arbitrary conditions, like requiring price to be non-negative, that every row must satisfy.

questions.question: What typically happens if you try to DROP a table that's referenced by a FOREIGN KEY in another table?
options: It always succeeds silently
The database usually blocks it unless the dependent constraint or data is handled first
The referencing table is automatically deleted too
Foreign keys are ignored during DROP
questions.explanation: Most databases prevent dropping a table that other tables still reference via foreign key, to avoid leaving broken references, unless you explicitly cascade or remove the dependency first.

questions.question: Why choose an appropriate column type (like DATE instead of TEXT for dates) when designing a schema?
options: Column types are purely cosmetic
Proper types enable correct sorting, validation, and date-specific functions that a generic TEXT column can't provide
TEXT columns are always faster
It's required for PRIMARY KEY to work
questions.explanation: Using the right type lets the database validate the data, sort it correctly, and support type-specific operations (like date arithmetic) that a generic TEXT column wouldn't support reliably.

lessons.title: Transactions & ACID
lessons.description: Group several changes into one all-or-nothing unit of work

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what a transaction is, why COMMIT/ROLLBACK matter, and what each ACID guarantee means in plain terms.

sections.title: 📦 Bundling changes together
🔐 ACID, in plain language
sections.content:
ACID is the set of guarantees a database makes about transactions:

• **Atomicity** — all the statements in the transaction succeed together, or none of them do
• **Consistency** — the database moves from one valid state to another; constraints are never violated, even mid-transaction
• **Isolation** — one transaction's in-progress changes don't leak into another transaction that's running at the same time
• **Durability** — once a transaction commits, it survives — even a crash right afterward won't lose it

You don't need to memorize the acronym — just remember the core idea: **a transaction is a promise that a group of changes either all happen, or none do.**

sections.title: ↩️ Why ROLLBACK matters
Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to COMMIT, leaving changes stuck in an open transaction that nobody else can see yet. Assuming every single individual statement is automatically its own safe transaction — for a sequence of related changes, you need an explicit BEGIN...COMMIT around all of them together.

questions.question: What does a transaction guarantee about a group of statements between BEGIN and COMMIT?
options: Each statement runs independently and can partially succeed
They all succeed together, or none of them take effect — it's all-or-nothing
Only the first statement is guaranteed to run
They run in a random order for performance
questions.explanation: The core promise of a transaction is atomicity: the whole group of changes is treated as a single unit that either fully commits or has no effect at all.

questions.question: What does ROLLBACK do?
options: Permanently saves all changes since BEGIN
Undoes every change made since BEGIN, as if the transaction never happened
Deletes the entire table
Restarts the database
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK cancels an in-progress transaction, reverting any changes made since BEGIN back to how things were before it started.

questions.question: In the ACID guarantees, which one ensures that once a transaction commits, it survives even a crash right after?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
questions.explanation: Durability is specifically the guarantee that committed changes are permanent — they won't be lost even if the system crashes immediately afterward.

questions.question: Which ACID property ensures other transactions don't see a transaction's partial, uncommitted changes?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
questions.explanation: Isolation ensures that concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other by seeing incomplete or intermediate changes from a transaction still in progress.

questions.question: Which ACID property ensures a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints?
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
questions.explanation: Consistency means a transaction can only bring the database from one valid state to another, never violating defined constraints and rules.

questions.question: What does COMMIT do?
options: Undoes all changes since BEGIN
Makes all changes made since BEGIN permanent
Deletes the transaction log
Locks the table permanently
questions.explanation: COMMIT finalizes every change made during the transaction, making it permanent and visible to other transactions.

questions.question: Why are transactions important when transferring money between two bank accounts (debit one, credit another)?
options: They aren't important — each statement can run independently
Without a transaction, a crash between the debit and credit could leave money missing or duplicated
Transactions make the transfer happen twice
Only SELECT statements need transactions
questions.explanation: Wrapping both statements in a transaction ensures they either both succeed or both fail together, preventing a crash from leaving the accounts in an inconsistent state.

questions.question: What's a real risk of NOT using a transaction for a multi-step operation that must succeed or fail as a unit?
options: The operation runs faster
A failure partway through could leave the database in an inconsistent, half-updated state
SQL automatically prevents partial updates without transactions
There is no risk
questions.explanation: Without a transaction wrapping related statements, a failure partway through can leave some changes applied and others not, resulting in inconsistent data.

lessons.title: Indexes & Query Performance
lessons.description: Understand why some queries are slow, and how an index speeds them up

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what an index does, when it helps, and read a basic EXPLAIN plan.

sections.title: 🔎 Why some queries are slow
sections.content: Without any help, a database answers `WHERE email = 'sam@example.com'` by checking **every single row**, one at a time — this is called a **full table scan**. On a small table that's instant; on a table with millions of rows, it can take real time.

sections.title: 📇 Indexes: a shortcut to the right rows
sections.content:
An **index** is a separate, sorted structure the database maintains alongside a table, built on one or more columns — think of it like the index at the back of a book, letting you jump straight to the right page instead of reading cover to cover:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_email ON customers (email);
```

Now a lookup by email can jump almost straight to the matching row instead of scanning the whole table. Primary keys and (usually) foreign keys are indexed automatically by most databases; other columns you query often — especially in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY — are good candidates to index explicitly.

sections.title: ⚖️ The tradeoff: indexes aren't free
sections.content:
Indexes speed up reads, but they come at a cost:

• Extra storage space, since the index is a separate structure
• Slower writes, since every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE has to keep the index up to date too

That's why you don't index *every* column "just in case" — the right approach is to index columns you actually filter, join, or sort by frequently, and skip the rest.

sections.title: 🩻 A quick look at EXPLAIN
sections.content:
Most databases let you preview how a query will actually run with `EXPLAIN`:

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = 'sam@example.com';
```

The output shows whether the database plans to use an index (fast) or scan the whole table (slow) for that query. You don't need to master every detail of an EXPLAIN plan right away — just knowing it exists, and roughly what "index scan" vs "full table scan" mean, already puts you ahead.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Adding an index to every column without a real reason, which slows down writes for little benefit. Expecting an index to help a query that doesn't actually filter, join, or sort on the indexed column.

questions.question: What's a full table scan?
options: A special kind of index
The database checking every row one by one, because it has no faster way to find the matching rows
A backup of the entire table
A syntax error
questions.explanation: Without an index to jump to the right rows, the database has no choice but to examine every row to find matches — that's a full table scan, and it gets slow on large tables.

questions.question: What's the tradeoff of adding an index?
options: Indexes have no downside — always add as many as possible
Indexes speed up matching reads, but cost extra storage and slow down writes, since the index must stay up to date
Indexes only work on primary keys
Indexes make SELECT * FROM slower
questions.explanation: An index speeds up lookups that use it, but every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE also has to update the index, and the index itself takes extra disk space — so indexes should be added deliberately, not everywhere.

questions.question: What does EXPLAIN show you about a query?
options: The exact rows it will return
How the database plans to execute the query — for example, whether it will use an index or scan the whole table
The query's syntax errors
A backup of the query's results
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN reveals the database's execution plan for a query, which is how you can confirm whether it's using an index efficiently or falling back to a slow full table scan.

questions.question: What kind of column is typically the best candidate for an index?
options: A column that's rarely used in WHERE or JOIN conditions
A column frequently used in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, or ORDER BY
A column with the same value in every row
Any column, regardless of usage
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up lookups on columns that are frequently filtered, joined on, or sorted by — indexing rarely-queried columns wastes storage and write performance for no benefit.

questions.question: Why does a PRIMARY KEY column usually already have an index automatically?
options: It doesn't — you must always add one manually
Because most databases automatically create an index to enforce the uniqueness and fast lookup PRIMARY KEY requires
Because PRIMARY KEY columns can't be indexed
Indexes only apply to TEXT columns
questions.explanation: Databases typically create an index automatically on a PRIMARY KEY to efficiently enforce uniqueness and support fast lookups by that key.

questions.question: What can happen if you add too many indexes to a heavily-written table?
options: Reads become instant with no downside
Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE has to update all those indexes too, slowing down writes
Indexes are automatically limited to one per table
Nothing changes for writes
questions.explanation: Every index must be kept in sync with the table's data, so each write operation has more work to do as more indexes are added, which can slow writes noticeably.

questions.question: If EXPLAIN shows a query is doing a full table scan despite a WHERE clause on an indexed column, what might be happening?
options: The index is guaranteed to be used regardless
The query planner may have decided a scan is cheaper, or the WHERE condition doesn't match the index well (e.g. using a function on the column)
EXPLAIN always lies about scans
Full table scans never happen with an index present
questions.explanation: A query planner can choose a full scan over an index if it estimates it's cheaper, or if the WHERE clause applies a function or pattern that prevents the index from being used effectively.

questions.question: What's a composite (multi-column) index useful for?
options: Indexing a single column twice
Speeding up queries that filter or sort on multiple specific columns together, in that order
Only usable for PRIMARY KEY columns
Replacing the need for any single-column indexes
questions.explanation: A composite index on multiple columns can speed up queries that filter or sort using that specific combination and order of columns together.

lessons.title: Capstone: A Real Business Report
lessons.description: Combine everything from this course into one realistic, multi-part report query

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write a multi-CTE report query that combines joins, aggregation, and a window function to answer a realistic business question.

sections.title: 🎓 The question
sections.content: "For each product category, show total revenue, and highlight the single best-selling product in that category." This one question needs nearly everything from this course: joins across four tables, aggregation, and a window function — a genuine test of everything you've learned.

sections.title: 🧱 Building it step by step with CTEs
sections.content:
Rather than one giant tangled query, build it as a chain of named steps — exactly the CTE pattern from the subqueries module:

```sql
WITH line_revenue AS (
  SELECT oi.product_id, p.category, p.name AS product_name,
         oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS revenue
  FROM order_items AS oi
  JOIN products AS p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
),
product_totals AS (
  SELECT category, product_name, SUM(revenue) AS product_revenue
  FROM line_revenue
  GROUP BY category, product_name
),
ranked_products AS (
  SELECT category, product_name, product_revenue,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY category ORDER BY product_revenue DESC
         ) AS rank_in_category,
         SUM(product_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category) AS category_revenue
  FROM product_totals
)
SELECT category, category_revenue, product_name AS best_seller, product_revenue
FROM ranked_products
WHERE rank_in_category = 1
ORDER BY category_revenue DESC;
```

sections.title: 🗺️ Tracing the logic
sections.content:
Each CTE has exactly one job:

• `line_revenue` — compute revenue per order line, with the product's category attached
• `product_totals` — GROUP BY to get total revenue per product
• `ranked_products` — a window function ranks products within each category, and another totals up the whole category's revenue
• the final `SELECT` keeps only rank 1 (the best seller) per category

This is exactly how experienced SQL users tackle a complex report: break it into small, named, individually understandable steps, and let the final query just pick from the last one.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Trying to write this as one giant nested query instead of breaking it into CTEs — it becomes far harder to debug and to reason about. Forgetting that a window function's PARTITION BY needs to match the grouping level you actually care about (here, category).

questions.question: In the capstone query, what is the job of the line_revenue CTE?
options: Rank products within each category
Compute revenue per individual order line item, along with the product's category
Filter to only the best-selling product
Calculate a running total by date
questions.explanation: line_revenue is the first step: it joins order_items to products and computes quantity * unit_price for each line, tagging each with its category — the raw material the later steps build on.

questions.question: Why does the query use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY product_revenue DESC) rather than just MAX(product_revenue)?
options: MAX would be identical here in every way
ROW_NUMBER lets the final query also keep the product's name and other columns for the top row per category, not just the maximum number
ROW_NUMBER is required whenever PARTITION BY is used
MAX() cannot be used inside a CTE
questions.explanation: MAX(product_revenue) alone would only give you the top number, not which product it belongs to. Ranking with ROW_NUMBER lets you filter down to the full row — product name and all — for the top-ranked entry in each category.

questions.question: Why is breaking this report into three chained CTEs (line_revenue, product_totals, ranked_products) a good approach?
options: It's required by SQL syntax
It makes each step individually simple to write, test, and understand, instead of one large tangled query
It runs faster than any other approach in every database
CTEs are the only way to use a window function
questions.explanation: Chaining small, clearly-named CTEs mirrors how you'd reason through the problem by hand — each step does one understandable thing, which makes the whole query far easier to write correctly and to debug later.

questions.question: In a report like the capstone's, why compute line_revenue as its own CTE before aggregating?
options: It's not necessary — the final aggregation could skip it
It isolates the per-line-item calculation (quantity x price) cleanly before summing it up by product or category
CTEs are required for SUM to work
It deletes duplicate order lines
questions.explanation: Separating the row-level revenue calculation into its own CTE keeps that logic simple and testable before the next step aggregates it further.

questions.question: Why might a capstone-style report combine JOIN, GROUP BY, and a window function in one query?
options: Because SQL requires using every feature in one query
Because real business questions often need combining tables, aggregating values, and then ranking or comparing those aggregates
Window functions can't be used with JOIN or GROUP BY otherwise
It's purely for style, with no functional reason
questions.explanation: Real-world reporting questions often need to combine data from multiple tables, summarize it, and then rank or compare those summaries — which naturally uses JOIN, GROUP BY, and window functions together.

questions.question: If the goal is 'top-selling product per category', what does filtering on a rank of 1 accomplish after using ROW_NUMBER() PARTITION BY category?
options: It removes all data
It keeps only the single highest-revenue product within each category
It keeps every product tied for any rank
It's unrelated to the goal
questions.explanation: Once each product is ranked within its category by revenue, filtering to rank = 1 leaves exactly one row per category — the top performer.

questions.question: Why is it useful to build a report step-by-step with intermediate CTEs rather than testing only the final query?
options: It's not useful — only the final result matters
You can inspect each CTE's output individually to catch mistakes early, before they compound in later steps
CTEs can't be tested individually
It doubles the runtime unnecessarily
questions.explanation: Checking each CTE's output as you build lets you catch errors in an early step before they silently propagate and produce a wrong final result.

questions.question: What broader SQL skill does writing a multi-CTE business report exercise most directly?
options: Memorizing keyword syntax alone
Decomposing a real business question into a sequence of clear, verifiable query steps
Avoiding the use of JOIN
Formatting output for spreadsheets
questions.explanation: The capstone exercises the practical skill of breaking a real-world question down into ordered, understandable query steps rather than one large, opaque statement.
